div.p: The wife of the worthy Phocion used to say that her ornament was the military achievements of Phocion; but I consider not merely my own private ornament, but the common ornament of all my household, to be my teacher's devotion to learning. For the most illustrious exploits of generals we know to be causes of safety from immediate dangers only for a few soldiers, or a single city, or at most a single nation, while in no way making either the soldiers or the citizens—or even their fellow countrymen—better men; whereas education, being the essence of happiness and the cause of sound counsel, is found to be useful not only to a household, a city, or a nation, but to the entire human race. In proportion, then, as the benefit of education is greater than all military exploits, so much the more is the record of it worthy of earnest study.

Now on the second day of the Saturnalia, the noble Onesicrates had invited to a banquet men
versed in music: these were Soterichus of Alexandria and Lysias, one of those who received a stipend from him. When the customary rites had been completed, What the cause of the human voice is, my friends, he said, is not a suitable inquiry for a drinking-party, for that question requires more sober leisure; but since the best grammarians define voice as struck air perceptible to hearing, and we happened yesterday to inquire into grammar as an art fitted to shape utterances by letters and store them up for recollection, let us see what second science after this befits the voice. I think it is music. For it is pious and a foremost duty for human beings to hymn the gods who have bestowed articulate voice upon them alone; and Homer too has indicated this where he says:
All day long they propitiated the god with song,
singing the fair paean, the youths of the Achaeans,
hymning the Far-Worker; and he rejoiced in his heart as he heard. Come then, devotees of music, remind our companions who first practiced music, what time has discovered for its advancement, who have been renowned among those who cultivated the science of music, and furthermore for how many purposes and to what ends this pursuit is useful. Thus spoke my teacher.

Lysias took up the discourse and said: By many
has this question been investigated which you raise, good Onesicrates; for most of the Platonists and the best of the Peripatetic philosophers have been eager to write treatises on ancient music and on the corruption that has befallen it; moreover, those among grammarians and harmonic theorists who have reached the summit of learning have devoted much study to this subject. Great, indeed, is the disagreement among the writers. Heraclides, in his Collection of Musical Matters, says that singing to the cithara and citharodic poetry were first invented by Amphion, the son of Zeus and Antiope, his father evidently having taught him. He confirms this from the register preserved at Sicyon, through which he names the priestesses at Argos, the poets, and the musicians. In the same era, he says, Linus of Euboea composed dirges, Anthes of Anthedon in Boeotia composed hymns, and Pierus of Pieria composed the poems about the Muses; furthermore, Philammon of Delphi set forth in song the birth of Leto, Artemis, and Apollo, and was the first to establish choruses around the sanctuary at Delphi; Thamyris, a Thracian by birth, sang with a sweeter voice and more melodiously than all men of that time, so that according to the poets he entered into a contest with the Muses, and he is recorded to have composed a War of the Titans against the Gods.
There was also Demodocus of Corcyra, an ancient musician, who composed a Sack of Troy and a Marriage of Aphrodite and Hephaestus; and Phemius of Ithaca composed a Return of those who came back from Troy with Agamemnon. The diction of the poems of the aforementioned was not unbound and lacking meter, but like that of Stesichorus and the ancient lyric poets, who composed hexameters and set melodies to them. For he said that Terpander, being a composer of citharodic nomes, set melodies to his own hexameters and to those of Homer for each nome and sang them in the contests; and he says that Terpander was the first to assign names to the citharodic nomes. Like Terpander, Clonas—who first established the aulodic nomes and the processional songs—was a poet of elegies and hexameters; and Polymnestus of Colophon, who came after him, used the same poetic forms.

p.q:
Now the aulodic nomes of their time, good Onesicrates, were Apothetus, Elegoi, Comarchius, Schoenion, Cepion, Deius, and Trimeles; and at a later time the so-called Polymnastia were also invented. The citharodic nomes, however, were established much earlier than the aulodic
in the time of Terpander; he at any rate was the first to name the citharodic nomes, calling them Boeotian, Aeolian, Trochaic, Sharp, Cepion, Terpandrean, and also Tetraoidios. Terpander also composed citharodic preludes in hexameters. That the ancient citharodic nomes were composed of hexameters was shown by Timotheus: he sang his earliest nomes in hexameters mixed with dithyrambic diction, so that he might not immediately appear to be violating the laws of ancient music. Terpander seems to have excelled in the citharodic art, for he is recorded as having won four consecutive victories at the Pythian games. In date too he is very ancient: Glaucus of Italy, in a treatise On the Ancient Poets and Musicians, declares him older than Archilochus; for he says that he came second after the first composers of aulody.

Alexander, in his Collection of Phrygian Affairs, said that Olympus was the first to bring instrumental music to the Greeks, as did also the Idaean Dactyls; that Hyagnis was the first to play the aulos, then his son Marsyas, and then Olympus; and that Terpander emulated Homer in his verses and Orpheus in his melodies. Orpheus, however, appears to have imitated no one, for no one had yet appeared before him except the composers of aulodic
songs, and the Orphic art resembles these in no respect. Clonas, the composer of aulodic nomes, who lived a little later than Terpander, was according to the Arcadians a Tegean, and according to the Boeotians a Theban. After Terpander and Clonas, Archilochus is handed down as having lived. Certain other writers say that Ardalus of Troezen established the aulodic art before Clonas; and that there was also a poet Polymnestus, son of Meles of Colophon, who composed the Polymnestus and Polymneste nomes. Regarding Clonas, the chroniclers record that he composed the Apothetus and Schoenion nomes; while Polymnestus is mentioned by both Pindar and Alcman, the lyric poets. Some of the citharodic nomes composed by Terpander are said to have been originated by the ancient Philammon of Delphi.

In general, citharody from Terpander down to the time of Phrynis remained altogether simple; for in ancient times it was not permitted to compose citharodies as is done now, nor to modulate harmonies and rhythms, since in each nome they preserved its proper pitch. Hence indeed they bore this name: they were called nomoi ("laws"), because it was not permitted to transgress the prescribed form of pitch for each. Having paid their due reverence to the gods as they wished,
they passed immediately to the poetry of Homer and the other poets, as is clear from the preludes of Terpander. The design of the cithara was first perfected under Cepion, the pupil of Terpander, and it was called the Asias because the Lesbian citharodes who dwelt near Asia used it. The last Lesbian citharode to win the Carneia at Lacedaemon is said to have been Periclitus; upon his death, the continuous succession of Lesbian citharody came to an end. Some mistakenly suppose that Hipponax lived at the same time as Terpander; yet even Periclitus appears to be older than Hipponax.

Since we have described the ancient aulodic and citharodic nomes together, we shall now pass to the aulodic and auletic nomes alone. It is said that the aforementioned Olympus, an aulete from Phrygia, composed an auletic nome in honor of Apollo called the Many-Headed; and they say this Olympus was one of the descendants of the first Olympus, the pupil of Marsyas, who composed the nomes to the gods. For this first Olympus, having been the beloved of Marsyas and having learned aulos-playing from him, brought the harmonic nomes to Greece, which the Greeks still use
at the festivals of the gods. Others say that the Many-Headed nome is by Crates, who was a pupil of Olympus, while Pratinas says this nome belongs to the younger Olympus. The nome called the Chariot nome is said to have been composed by the first Olympus, the pupil of Marsyas. Some say Marsyas was called Masses; others deny this and say he was Marsyas, son of Hyagnis, who first invented the art of playing the aulos. That the Chariot nome is by Olympus one may learn from Glaucus's treatise on the ancient poets, and one may further learn that Stesichorus of Himera imitated neither Orpheus nor Terpander nor Archilochus nor Thaletas, but Olympus, employing the Chariot nome and the dactylic form, which some say derives from the Orthian nome. Certain others say this nome was invented by the Mysians, for there were certain ancient Mysian auletes.

There is also another ancient nome called Cradias, which Hipponax says Mimnermus played on the aulos. For originally the aulodes sang elegies set to music, as is shown by the Panathenaic register concerning the musical contest. There was also Sacadas of Argos, a composer of lyric songs and of elegies set to music;
he was both a good poet and is recorded as having won three victories at the Pythian games, and Pindar mentions him. There being three modes according to Polymnestus and Sacadas—the Dorian, Phrygian, and Lydian—they say Sacadas composed a strophe in each of these modes and taught the chorus to sing the first in Dorian, the second in Phrygian, and the third in Lydian; and this nome was called Tripartite because of the modulation. In the Sicyonian register of poets, however, Clonas is recorded as the inventor of the Tripartite nome.

Now the first establishment of musical affairs at Sparta took place under Terpander; of the second, Thaletas of Gortyn, Xenodamus of Cythera, Xenocritus of Locri, Polymnestus of Colophon, and Sacadas of Argos are chiefly credited with having been the leaders. Through their introduction, the Gymnopaediae at Lacedaemon are said to have been established, as well as the Apodeixeis in Arcadia and the so-called Endymatia at Argos. Thaletas, Xenodamus, and Xenocritus were composers of paeans; Polymnestus of the so-called Orthian songs; and Sacadas of elegies. Others say that Xenodamus was a composer of hyporchemata rather than paeans, as Pratinas states; and indeed a song of
Xenodamus himself is remembered which is clearly a hyporchema. Pindar also used this genre of poetry; and that the paean differs from hyporchemata is shown by Pindar's poems, for he wrote both paeans and hyporchemata.

Polymnestus too composed aulodic nomes; whether he used melody in the Orthian nome, as the harmonic theorists say, we cannot state with certainty, for the ancients have said nothing about this. About Thaletas of Crete too it is disputed whether he was a composer of paeans. For Glaucus, asserting that Thaletas lived after Archilochus, says that he imitated the melodies of Archilochus but extended them to greater length, and introduced the Maron and Cretic rhythms into his melodic composition—rhythms used neither by Archilochus nor by Orpheus nor by Terpander; for they say Thaletas developed these from the aulos-playing of Olympus and gained a reputation as a fine poet. As for Xenocritus, who was by birth from Locri in Italy, it is disputed whether he was a composer of paeans, for they say he composed heroic subjects involving action, which is why some call his pieces dithyrambs;
and Glaucus says Thaletas was older than Xenocritus.

Olympus, as Aristoxenus says, is regarded by musicians as the inventor of the enharmonic genus; for everything before him was diatonic and chromatic. They suppose the discovery happened somewhat as follows: while working in the diatonic genus and frequently bringing the melody down to the diatonic parhypate, sometimes from paramese and sometimes from mese, and skipping over the diatonic lichanos, Olympus observed the beauty of the resulting character; admiring and adopting the scale thus formed by analogy, he composed in it in the Dorian mode, touching neither the notes peculiar to the diatonic nor those of the chromatic, but already those of the enharmonic. Such were his first enharmonic pieces. They place first among these the Spondeios, in which none of the divisions exhibits its own distinctive character, unless someone looking at the higher spondeiasmos conjectures that this itself is diatonic. Yet it is clear that anyone who assumes this will assert what is both false and unmelodic: false, because it is smaller by a diesis than the tone lying adjacent to the leading note; and unmelodic, because even if one were to assign to the higher spondeiasmos the value of a tone,
it would follow that two ditones would be placed in succession, one incomposite and the other composite. For the enharmonic pyknon in the middle tetrachord, which is now used, does not seem to belong to this composer; this is easy to perceive if one listens to someone playing the aulos in the archaic style, for it requires the semitone in the middle tetrachord to be incomposite as well. Such, then, were the first enharmonic pieces; later the semitone was divided in both the Lydian and Phrygian modes. Thus Olympus evidently advanced music by introducing something previously nonexistent and unknown to his predecessors, and became the founder of noble Greek music.

There is also an account concerning rhythms; for certain genera and species of rhythms were subsequently invented, as well as of melodic and rhythmic compositions. First, Terpander's innovation introduced a noble style into music; Polymnestus followed the Terpandrean style, which he also used, while himself too keeping to the noble pattern; and likewise Thaletas and Sacadas, for they too were skilled in rhythmic composition without departing from the noble pattern. There is also an Alcmanic
and a Stesichorean innovation, these too not departing from the noble. Crexus, however, and Timotheus, Philoxenus, and the poets of their generation became more vulgar and fond of novelty, pursuing the style now called "philanthropic" and "thematic"; for fewness of strings, simplicity, and dignity in music have come to be regarded as completely archaic.

div.p: Having spoken to the best of my ability about the earliest music, its first inventors, and by whom it was advanced over time through further discoveries, I shall conclude my speech and yield the floor to our companion Soterichus, who has devoted himself not only to music but also to the rest of liberal education; for I myself have been trained rather in the practical part of music. With these words Lysias concluded his speech.

After him, Soterichus spoke somewhat as follows: It is on a noble pursuit, and one most pleasing to the gods, good Onesicrates, that you have urged us to discourse. I commend our teacher Lysias for his intelligence, and also for the memory he has displayed regarding the inventors of early music and those who have written about such matters; yet I would remind you that he has made his exposition following written records alone.
We, however, have received by tradition no human being as the inventor of the blessings of music, but Apollo, the god adorned with every virtue. For the aulos is not the invention of Marsyas, Olympus, or Hyagnis, as some suppose; nor is the cithara alone Apollo's, but the god is the inventor of both auletics and citharistics. This is clear from the dances and sacrifices that men offered to the god with auloi, as Alcaeus among others relates in one of his hymns. Moreover, the consecration of his statue on Delos holds a bow in its right hand and the Graces in its left, each holding a musical instrument: one holds a lyre, another auloi, and the one in the middle holds a syrinx to her lips. That this account is not my own, Anticles and Ister have related in their Epiphanies. And so ancient is this statue that its makers are said to have been among the Meropes of Heracles' time. Furthermore, the boy who brings the laurel from Tempe to Delphi is accompanied by an aulete; and the sacred offerings from the Hyperboreans are said to have been sent of old to Delos with auloi, syringes, and cithara. Others say that the god himself played the aulos, as the finest lyric poet Alcman relates; and Corinna even says that Apollo was taught to play the aulos by Athena. Noble in every respect, then, is music, being the invention of the gods.

p.q: The ancients made use of it as befitted its worth, just as with all other pursuits; but men of today, rejecting its dignified elements, instead of that manly, inspired, and god-beloved music, introduce into the theaters a broken and chattering style. Therefore Plato in the third book of the Republic expresses distaste for such music: he rejects the Lydian harmony because it is high-pitched and suited to lamentation. Indeed, its very first origin is said to have been lamentatory; for Aristoxenus in the first book of his On Music says that Olympus first played a dirge on the aulos in the Lydian mode over the Python. Some say Melanippides began this melody, while Pindar in his Paeans says the Lydian harmony was first taught at the marriage of Niobe, and others say Torebus first used the harmony, as Dionysius the Iambus relates.

The Mixolydian too is emotional and suited to tragedies. Aristoxenus says that Sappho was the first to invent the Mixolydian, from whom the tragic poets learned it; taking it over, they coupled it with the Dorian, since the latter gives magnificence and dignity while the former gives emotion, and tragedy is a blend of these. In his Historical Notes on Harmonics, however, he says Pythoclides the aulete was its inventor;
while Lysis says that Lamprocles of Athens, perceiving that it does not have its disjunction where nearly everyone supposed, but toward the higher end, gave it the form extending from paramese to hypate hypaton. Furthermore, they say that the Relaxed Lydian, being opposite to the Mixolydian and closely akin to the Ionian, was invented by Damon of Athens.

Since, then, one of these harmonies is lamentatory and the other relaxed, Plato reasonably rejected them and chose the Dorian as suited to warlike and temperate men—not, by Zeus, out of ignorance, as Aristoxenus says in the second book of his Musical Works, that there was something useful in the others as well for the guardianship of states; for Plato paid close attention to the science of music, having been a pupil of Draco of Athens and Metellus of Acragas. Rather, since, as we said before, there is much dignity in the Dorian, he preferred it. He was not unaware that many Dorian maiden-songs were composed by Alcman, Pindar, Simonides, and Bacchylides, as well as processional songs and paeans, and indeed that tragic laments and some love songs were sometimes sung in the Dorian mode; yet the songs to Ares and Athena and the spondaic pieces sufficed for him, for these are capable of strengthening
the soul of a temperate man. Nor was he ignorant of the Lydian and the Ionian, for he knew that tragedy employed this kind of melodic composition.

All the ancients too, though not unacquainted with all the harmonies, made use of only some of them; for it was not ignorance that caused this narrow compass and fewness of strings among them, nor was it through ignorance that Olympus, Terpander, and those who followed their deliberate choice excluded multiplicity of strings and elaboration. The compositions of Olympus, Terpander, and all who shared their style bear witness to this: though few-stringed and simple, they so surpass the elaborate and many-stringed compositions that no one can imitate the style of Olympus, and those who occupy themselves with many strings and many styles fall short of him.

That the ancients did not abstain from trite in the spondaic style out of ignorance is made clear by their use of it in instrumental accompaniment; for they would never have used it in consonance with parhypate had they not known its use. Rather, it is evident that the character of beauty produced in the spondaic style by the omission of trite was what led their perception to carry the melody directly to paranete. The same argument applies to nete: for this too they used in
accompaniment, both in dissonance with paranete and in consonance with mese, yet in melody it did not seem to them suited to the spondaic style. Nor did they use only these notes thus, but also nete synemmenon: in accompaniment they sounded it in dissonance with paranete and paramese, and in consonance with mese and lichanos, whereas in melody anyone who used it would have been ashamed of the character produced by it. It is clear from the Phrygian pieces as well that it was not unknown to Olympus and his followers, for they used it not only in accompaniment but also in melody in the Mother-goddess hymns and in some of the Phrygian pieces. The same is clear regarding the hypate tetrachord—that they did not abstain from this tetrachord in Dorian pieces out of ignorance: in fact they used it in the other modes, obviously knowing it, but for the sake of preserving the character they omitted it in the Dorian mode, honoring its beauty.

Much the same holds for the tragic poets: for tragedy has never down to this day used the chromatic genus or its rhythm, whereas the cithara, which is many generations older than tragedy,
used it from the beginning. That the chromatic is older than the enharmonic is clear; for of course one must speak of "older" with respect to human discovery and use, since in the nature of the genera themselves one is not older than another. If, then, anyone should say that Aeschylus or Phrynichus abstained from the chromatic out of ignorance, would he not be absurd? For the same person might also say that Pancrates was ignorant of the chromatic genus, since he too for the most part abstained from it, yet used it in certain pieces; obviously, then, he abstained not out of ignorance, but by deliberate choice, for as he himself said, he emulated the style of Pindar and Simonides, and in general what men of today call the ancient style.

The same argument holds for Tyrtaeus of Mantinea, Andreas of Corinth, Thrasyllus of Phlius, and many others, all of whom we know to have abstained by deliberate choice from the chromatic, modulation, multiplicity of strings, and many other commonly available rhythms, harmonies, dictions, melodic compositions, and styles of delivery. For instance, Telephanes of Megara was so hostile to the syrinx-holes that he never even allowed the aulos-makers to put them on his auloi, and it was chiefly on this account that he stayed away from the Pythian contest. In general, if anyone judges from non-use that those who do not use a thing are ignorant of it, he will end up condemning many
of our contemporaries too—for example, the followers of Dorion who despise the style of Antigenidas because they do not use it, the followers of Antigenidas who despise that of Dorion for the same reason, and the citharodes who despise the style of Timotheus, having practically deserted to patchwork pieces and the poems of Polyeidus. Again, if one examines elaboration properly and with experience, comparing past and present, one would find that elaboration was in use then too: for the ancients employed a more elaborate variety in rhythmic composition—they prized rhythmic variety, and instrumental styles too were then more varied, since men of today are lovers of melody whereas those of old were lovers of rhythm. It is clear, then, that the ancients abstained from broken melodies not out of ignorance, but by deliberate choice. And why should that be surprising? Many other practices of life as well are not unknown to practitioners, yet have been discarded and their use abandoned because they are unseemly for certain purposes.

Now that it has been shown that Plato rejected the other modes not out of ignorance or inexperience, but as unsuited to such a state, we shall next show that he was well versed in harmonics. In the generation of the soul in the
Timaeus, he displayed his devotion to mathematics and music as follows: And after this he filled up both the double and the triple intervals, cutting off further portions from the same mixture and placing them in the intervals between them, so that in each interval there were two means. This opening passage belongs to harmonic science, as we shall immediately show. There are three primary means, from which every mean is derived: the arithmetic, the harmonic, and the geometric. Of these, one exceeds and is exceeded by an equal number, another by an equal ratio, and the third by neither the same ratio nor the same number. Wishing, then, to show harmonically the psychic harmony of the four elements and the cause of their mutual consonance out of unlike parts, Plato posited two psychic means in each interval according to musical ratio. For in music the consonance of the octave happens to have two intermediate intervals, whose proportion we shall demonstrate. The octave is observed in the double ratio; by way of illustration, the numbers six and twelve will produce the double ratio, and this is the interval from hypate meson to nete diezeugmenon. With six and twelve as the extremes, hypate meson has the number six, and nete diezeugmenon has the number twelve. It remains to take the numbers falling between these, to which the extremes will stand in the ratios of four to three and three to two: these are
eight and nine; for of six, eight is four-thirds and nine is three-halves. Such is the relation to one extreme; and as for the other extreme, twelve, it is four-thirds of nine and three-halves of eight. With these numbers lying between six and twelve, and the octave interval being composed of the fourth and the fifth, it is clear that mese will have the number eight and paramese the number nine. This being so, hypate will stand to mese as paramese stands to nete diezeugmenon; for from hypate meson to mese is a fourth, and from paramese to nete diezeugmenon is a fourth (completing the octave). The same proportion is found in the numbers too: as six is to eight, so nine is to twelve; and as six is to nine, so eight is to twelve—for eight is four-thirds of six and twelve is four-thirds of nine, while nine is three-halves of six and twelve is three-halves of eight. What has been said will suffice to demonstrate the zeal and expertise that Plato possessed in mathematics.

That harmony is something noble, divine, and great, Aristotle the pupil of Plato states in these words: Harmony is heavenly, possessing a divine, noble, and wondrous nature; being fourfold in its power by nature, it has two means, the arithmetic and the harmonic, and its parts,
magnitudes, and excesses are manifested according to number and equal measure, for melodies are ordered in two tetrachords. Those are his actual words. He also said that its body is composed of unlike parts that nevertheless agree with one another, and furthermore that its means agree according to arithmetic ratio. For nete, tuned in the double ratio to hypate, produces the consonance of the octave: as we said before, nete has twelve units, hypate six, paramese—consonant with hypate in the three-halves ratio—has nine units, and mese, as we said, has eight units. Through these are constituted the chief intervals of music: the fourth, which is in the ratio of four to three; the fifth, which is in the ratio of three to two; and the octave, which is in the ratio of two to one; and moreover the ratio of nine to eight is preserved, which is the ratio of a tone. By the same excesses the parts of harmony exceed and are exceeded by one another, and the means by the means, both in numerical excess and in geometric power. Thus Aristotle shows that they possess these powers: nete exceeds mese by a third part of itself, and hypate is exceeded by paramese in the same proportion, so that the excesses are relative—for they exceed and are exceeded by the
same fractions, and the extremes exceed and are exceeded by mese and paramese in the same ratios, four-thirds and three-halves. Such, then, is the harmonic excess. On the other hand, the excess of nete over mese exhibits equal differences according to arithmetic ratio, and likewise paramese over hypate; paramese exceeds mese in the ratio of nine to eight; again, nete is double hypate, paramese is three-halves of hypate, and mese is tuned at four-thirds to hypate. Such, according to Aristotle too, is the nature of harmony in its parts and numbers.

Most naturally, both harmony itself and all its parts are composed of the unlimited, the limiting, and the even-odd nature. As a whole it is even, consisting of four terms, while its parts and ratios are even, odd, and even-odd: for it has nete even, of twelve units; paramese odd, of nine units; mese even, of eight units; and hypate even-odd, being of six units. Being thus constituted by nature, both in itself and in its parts
in relation to one another by their excesses and ratios, it is consonant as a whole with itself and with its parts.

Moreover, the senses implanted in bodies—those that are heavenly and divine, granting perception to human beings with God's aid through harmony, namely sight and hearing—reveal harmony through sound and light; and the other senses that attend upon them are also constituted according to harmony, for they too accomplish everything not without harmony, being inferior to the former yet not divorced from them; for the former, coming to bodies along with the presence of God according to reason, possess a strong and noble nature.

It is clear from this, then, that the ancient Greeks rightly cared above all else to be educated in music. For they thought it necessary to mold and attune the souls of the young to seemliness through music, since music is evidently useful for every occasion and every serious action, and above all for the perils of war. In war some used auloi, like the Lacedaemonians, among whom the so-called Castorean melody was played on the aulos whenever they marched in order to do battle with the enemy; others advanced against their foes to the sound of the lyre, as the Cretans are recorded to have long employed this manner of marching out to the perils of war; and still others even in our own day continue to use trumpets. The Argives used the aulos for the wrestling match of the festival called
Stheneia among them—a contest said to have been originally instituted under Danaus and later dedicated to Zeus Sthenius. Indeed, even today it is customary for pentathletes to be accompanied by the aulos—nothing choice or ancient, nor such as was customary among those men of old, like the piece composed by Hierax for this contest called Endrome—yet even though it is feeble and commonplace, the aulos is still played.

In still earlier times, however, they say the Greeks did not even know theatrical music, and the entire science was employed for the honor of the gods and the education of the young, since no theater had yet been built at all among those men, and music still had its home in the temples, where through it they rendered honor to the divine and praise to good men; indeed, it is likely that the word "theater" later, and "to behold" (theorein) much earlier, took their name from theos ("god"). In our own times, however, the form of corruption has advanced so far that there is no longer any mention or conception of the educational style, and all who engage in music have gone over to theatrical music.

Someone might ask: My good sir, did the ancients then invent and innovate nothing further? I myself affirm
that they did make further inventions, but with dignity and propriety. For those who have recorded such matters attributed to Terpander the Dorian nete, which his predecessors had not used in melody; and he is said to have invented the entire Mixolydian mode, as well as the style of Orthian melody corresponding to the Orthian rhythms, together with the marked trochee in addition to the Orthian. Furthermore, as Pindar says, Terpander was also the inventor of drinking-songs (skolia). Archilochus too invented the rhythmic composition of trimeters, the transition into rhythms of different genera, recitative delivery (parakataloge), and its instrumental accompaniment; to him first are attributed epodes, tetrameters, the cretic, the prosodiac, and the lengthening of the heroic verse—and by some also the elegiac—as well as the setting of the iambic to the epibatos paeon and of the lengthened heroic to the prosodiac and cretic. Moreover, they say Archilochus first introduced the practice of reciting some iambics to accompaniment and singing others, which the tragic poets then adopted, and Crexus took it over and brought it into use for dithyrambs. They also think he first invented accompaniment distinct from the vocal line, whereas all the ancients played note-for-note in unison.

To Polymnestus they attribute the mode now called Hypolydian, and say that he made the lowering (eklysis) and raising (ekbole) of pitch much greater. And to that same Olympus, to whom they assign the origin of Greek and nomic music, they attribute the invention of the enharmonic genus, and among rhythms the prosodiac—in which the Nome of Ares is set—and the choreios, which he used extensively in the Mother-goddess hymns; some also think Olympus invented the bacchius. Each of the ancient melodies shows that this is so. Lasus of Hermione, by transferring rhythms to the dithyrambic style and following the wide compass of the auloi, used more numerous and widely spaced notes, and thus brought about a transformation of the preexisting music.

Similarly Melanippides the lyric poet, coming later, did not abide by the preexisting music, nor did Philoxenus or Timotheus; for the latter, whereas the lyre had been seven-stringed down to Terpander of Antissa, scattered it into a greater number of notes. Indeed, aulos-playing too passed from a simpler to a more elaborate music: for
in ancient times, down to Melanippides the dithyrambic poet, it had been the custom for auletes to receive their pay from the poets—poetry obviously playing the leading role while the auletes served the chorus-masters; later this too was corrupted, so that Pherecrates the comic poet brought Music onto the stage in the guise of a woman whose entire body had been battered, and makes Justice inquire the cause of her outrage and Poetry (Music) reply:
MOUS. I will tell you not unwillingly; for your heart takes
pleasure in hearing, and mine in telling.
My troubles began with Melanippides,
who was the first to seize and loosen me
and make me slacker with his twelve strings.
Still, even so, he was a tolerable enough fellow
for me compared to my present woes.
Then Cinesias, that cursed Attic fellow,
making out-of-tune twists in his strophes,
so ruined me that in his dithyrambic
poetry, just as on shields,
his right side appears to be his left.
Yet even he was still bearable to me.
Next Phrynis, inserting a peculiar whirligig of his own,
bending and twisting me, ruined me completely,
cramming twelve harmonies into five strings.
Yet even he was a tolerable enough fellow for me,
for if he made a slip, he made up for it again.
But Timotheus, my dearest, has buried me alive
and shredded me most shamefully. DIK. Who is this
Timotheus? MOUS. A certain red-headed Milesian!
He has inflicted woes on me, surpassing all those I mention,
singing outlandish ant-tracks.
And if he ever meets me walking alone,
he strips me and unstrings me with his twelve strings! Aristophanes the comic poet also mentions Philoxenus and says that he introduced solo melodies into the circular choruses; and Music says this:
With out-of-tune, unholy hyperbolaean notes
and trills, just like a cabbage, he stuffed
me completely full of twists and bends. Other comic poets too exposed the absurdity of those who subsequently chopped music into tiny bits.

That improvement or perversion depends upon training and education
was made clear by Aristoxenus. For he says that among his contemporaries, Telesias of Thebes happened in his youth to be brought up in the finest music and to learn other esteemed works, especially those of Pindar, Dionysius of Thebes, Lamprus, Pratinas, and the rest of the lyric poets who were good composers of instrumental melodies; he also played the aulos well and trained thoroughly in the other branches of a complete education. Yet when he had passed his prime, he was so completely seduced by theatrical and elaborate music that he despised those noble works in which he had been reared and thoroughly learned those of Philoxenus and Timotheus—and of these the most elaborate and most full of innovation. Yet when he set out to compose melodies and tried both styles, the Pindaric and the Philoxenean, he was unable to succeed in the Philoxenean manner; and the cause was his noble training from childhood.

If anyone, then, wishes to practice music nobly and with discrimination, let him emulate the ancient style; yet let him also supplement it with the other sciences and set philosophy over it as a guide, for philosophy alone is capable of judging what measure is fitting
and useful in music. Since there are three parts into which all music is divided in its general division—diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic—one who approaches music must be knowledgeable in the poetry that employs these and competent in the performance that conveys what has been composed. First, then, we must recognize that all musical instruction is a habituation that has not yet grasped the reason why each thing taught must be learned by the student. Next we must reflect that no enumeration of styles is yet introduced into such training and instruction; rather, most people learn at random whatever pleases the teacher or the learner, whereas intelligent people reject randomness, as did the Lacedaemonians of old, the Mantineans, and the Pellenians—for selecting one style or very few that they judged suited to the improvement of character, they practiced that music alone.

This would become clear if one examined each of the sciences to see what it investigates: for it is evident that harmonics is the knowledge of the genera of the attuned, of intervals, scales, notes, modes, and modulations of scales;
beyond this it cannot go. Hence one must not even ask of it the ability to discern whether the poet has appropriately chosen, for example in the Mysians, the Hypodorian mode for the beginning, or the Mixolydian and Dorian for the conclusion, or the Hypophrygian and Phrygian for the middle. For the science of harmonics does not extend to such matters, and needs many other disciplines, since it is ignorant of the faculty of appropriateness. Neither the chromatic genus nor the enharmonic will ever come endowed with the complete power of appropriateness through which the character of a composed melody is revealed; rather, this is the work of the artist. It is clear, then, that the voice of a scale is one thing and that of the melody constructed within the scale is another, and it does not belong to the science of harmonics to investigate the latter. The same argument applies to rhythms: no rhythm will come having the power of complete appropriateness in itself, for whenever we speak of "appropriately" we always have regard to some character; and we say the cause of this is some composition or mixture, or both. For instance, in Olympus, the enharmonic genus set in the Phrygian mode and mixed with the epibatos paeon generated the character of the opening in the Nome of Athena; for when melodic and rhythmic composition were added,
and the rhythm alone was skillfully changed so as to become trochaic instead of paeonic, the enharmonic genus of Olympus came into being. Moreover, even while the enharmonic genus, the Phrygian mode, and the entire scale remain unchanged, the character has undergone a great alteration: for the so-called harmonia in the Nome of Athena differs greatly in character from the anapeira. If, therefore, critical judgment is added to musical experience, it is clear that such a person will be the true master in music; for one who knows the Dorian mode without knowing how to judge the appropriateness of its use will not know what he is doing, nor will he even preserve its character—since even concerning Dorian melodic compositions themselves it is disputed whether the science of harmonics can diagnose Dorian melodies, as some think, or not. The same holds for the whole science of rhythm: one who knows the paeon will not know the appropriateness of its use merely from knowing the construction of the paeon itself, since even concerning paeonic rhythmic compositions it is disputed whether the science of rhythm can diagnose them, as some say, or does not extend that far. At least two kinds of knowledge, then, are necessary for one who is to discern what is appropriate and what is alien: first, knowledge of the character for the sake of which
the composition has been made; and second, knowledge of the elements out of which the composition is formed. That neither harmonics nor rhythmics nor any other single partial science is self-sufficient on its own to recognize character and judge the rest, what has been said will suffice.

Although there are three genera into which the attuned is divided—equal in the sizes of their scales, in the functions of their notes, and likewise in those of their tetrachords—the ancients dealt with only one: for our predecessors investigated neither the chromatic nor the diatonic, but only the enharmonic, and of that again only a single scale magnitude, the so-called octave. They differed about its shades (chroai), but nearly all agreed that the enharmonic itself was one. One who has advanced only to this knowledge, then, could never grasp the full scope of harmonics, but only by following both the partial sciences and the entire body of music, together with the mixtures and combinations of its parts; for the mere harmonicist is circumscribed in a way. Speaking generally, both perception and intellect must keep pace together in
judging the parts of music, neither running ahead—as hasty and impetuous perceptions do—nor lagging behind, as slow and sluggish ones do. Sometimes in certain perceptions a combination of both occurs, so that the very same ones both lag behind and run ahead through some natural unevenness. Such defects must therefore be removed from a perception that is to keep pace.

For it is always necessary that at least three things fall simultaneously upon the ear: note, duration, and syllable or letter. From the progression of notes the attuned will be recognized, from that of durations the rhythm, and from that of letters or syllables the words; and as they advance together, perception must necessarily attend to them simultaneously. Yet this too is clear: if perception is unable to distinguish each of these elements, it cannot follow the details or discern what is faulty and what is not in each of them. First, then, one must understand continuity; for the critical faculty must necessarily possess continuity, since excellence and its opposite arise not in isolated notes, durations, or letters, but in continuous sequences, because there is a kind of mixture in the use of the incomposite elements. So much, then, concerning following music.

Next we must consider that men skilled in music are not self-sufficient for the task of criticism. For it is impossible to become a complete musician and critic solely from what are thought to be the parts of music as a whole—such as skill with instruments, singing, and training of perception (I mean that which contributes to understanding the attuned and rhythm), as well as rhythmics, harmonics, the theory of instrumental accompaniment and diction, and any other remaining branches. For what reasons one cannot become a critic from these alone we must try to learn. First, because some of the objects judged are complete and others incomplete: complete are each poem itself—whether sung, played on the aulos, or played on the cithara—and the performance of each, such as aulos-playing, singing, and the like; incomplete are the means contributing to these and done for their sake, namely the parts of performance. Second, from poetry itself, for it stands in the same case: one listening to an aulete may judge whether the auloi are in tune or not, and whether the articulation is clear or the reverse; each of these is a part
of auletic performance, yet not its end, only a means to the end. Beyond all these and such things, the character of the performance will be judged—whether it is rendered appropriately to the poem assigned, which the performer has undertaken to handle and interpret. And the same holds true for the emotions signified by the poetic art in the poems.

Since, then, the ancients made character their chief concern, they preferred the dignity and simplicity of ancient music. The Argives, indeed, are said once to have imposed a penalty on lawlessness in music and to have fined the first man who attempted to use more than seven strings among them and tried to modulate into the Mixolydian. And the venerable Pythagoras rejected the judgment of music through sense-perception, declaring that its excellence is grasped by the intellect; accordingly, he judged it not by hearing, but by proportional harmony, and considered it sufficient to fix the comprehension of music within the compass of the octave.

Men of today, however, have completely rejected the finest of the genera, the very one most prized by the ancients for its dignity, so that most people have not even the slightest perception of enharmonic intervals; and they are so lazy and careless that they think the enharmonic diesis does not even produce an impression
among perceptible things at all, banish it from their melodies, and claim that those who held any view on this subject and used this genus were talking nonsense. As the strongest proof that they speak the truth, they adduce first of all their own insensibility—as though whatever escapes them must thereby be completely nonexistent and useless—and second, the fact that this magnitude cannot be obtained through consonance, like the semitone, the tone, and other such intervals. They have failed to notice that on this basis the third, fifth, and seventh magnitudes would also be cast out—consisting of three, five, and seven dieses respectively—and in general all odd intervals would be rejected as useless inasmuch as none of them can be obtained through consonance, namely all those measured an odd number of times by the smallest diesis; from which it would necessarily follow that none of the divisions of the tetrachord is useful except only that which uses exclusively even intervals—namely, the tense diatonic and the tonic chromatic.

To say and suppose such things is not only to contradict the phenomena, but also to contradict themselves. For they themselves
evidently make greatest use of divisions of the tetrachord in which most of the intervals are either odd or irrational: they are always softening lichanoi and paranetai, and now they even lower some of the fixed notes, simultaneously lowering the tritai and paranetai by an irrational interval; and they think that use of scales most admirable in which most of the intervals are irrational, with not only the naturally movable notes but even some of the immovable ones lowered, as is clear to those able to perceive such things.

The proper use of music for a man was taught by the noble Homer; for showing that music is useful on many occasions, he represented Achilles digesting his anger against Agamemnon through the music he had learned from the most wise Chiron:
Him they found, he says, delighting his heart with the clear-toned lyre,
fair and richly wrought, with a silver crossbar upon it,
which he took from the spoils when he sacked the city of Eetion;
with this he delighted his soul, and sang the glories of men. Learn, says Homer, how one ought to use music; for to sing the glories of men and the deeds of demigods befitted Achilles, son of the most righteous Peleus. Teaching further the fitting occasion for its use,
Homer devised a useful and pleasant exercise for him while idle; for Achilles, being warlike and active, was taking no part in the perils of war because of his wrath against Agamemnon. Homer therefore judged it fitting for the hero to whet his soul with the noblest songs so that he might be prepared for the sally he was soon to make; and this he did clearly by recalling the deeds of old. Such was ancient music, and useful to this end. For we hear that Heracles, Achilles, and many others practiced music, whose educator is handed down to have been the most wise Chiron, teacher at once of music, justice, and medicine.

In general, a sensible man would surely not lay the blame upon the sciences if someone uses them improperly, but would consider this peculiar to the vice of those who use them. Accordingly, if someone has cultivated the educational style of music and received proper care in boyhood, he will praise and welcome what is noble and censure its opposite both in other matters and in music; such a man will be pure of every ignoble action, and having reaped the greatest benefit from music, will become a great boon both to himself and to his city, employing no discordant deed or word, and preserving always and everywhere what is fitting, temperate, and orderly.

div.p:
That the best-governed cities also took great care to foster noble music, many other testimonies can be cited to show; one might mention Terpander, who ended a civil strife that once arose among the Lacedaemonians, and Thaletas of Crete, who is said in accordance with a Pythian oracle to have come to Lacedaemon, healed them through music, and delivered Sparta from the plague that gripped it, as Pratinas relates. Indeed, Homer too says that the plague gripping the Greeks was halted through music; he said:
All day long they propitiated the god with song,
singing the fair paean, the youths of the Achaeans,
hymning the Far-Worker; and he rejoiced in his heart as he heard. These verses, good teacher, I have made the culmination of my discourse on music, since you first set forth the power of music to us through them. For in truth its first and fairest work is a grateful return to the gods; and next to this, and second, is the purifying, harmonious, and well-attuned ordering of the soul. Having said this, Soterichus added: There you have our general discourse on music, good teacher.

Soterichus was admired for what he had said, for he revealed his devotion to music both in his countenance and in his voice. Then my
teacher said: Among other things, I commend this in each of you, that each has kept to his own province: for Lysias has feasted us with all that it befits a practicing citharode alone to know, while Soterichus has regaled us generously by teaching everything that pertains to utility, theory, and indeed the power and use of music. One point, however, I think they have purposely left for me—for I will not accuse them of timidity, as if they were ashamed to bring music down to banquets—namely, that it is also useful over wine, as the noble Homer showed; for somewhere he says that song and dance—for these are the ornaments of a feast. Let no one suppose that Homer thought music useful solely for pleasure in these lines; rather, a deeper meaning lies hidden in the verses, for he introduced music as the greatest benefit and aid on those very occasions—I mean at the dinners and gatherings of the ancients. For it was customary to bring in music as capable of counteracting and soothing the heating power of wine, as your own Aristoxenus somewhere says; for he declared that music was introduced inasmuch as wine by nature causes the bodies and minds of those who partake of it freely to stumble, whereas music, by its own
order and proportion, leads them to the opposite state and calms them. On such an occasion, then, Homer says the ancients used music as a remedy.

Yet the greatest point of all, my friends, and the one that reveals music as most august, has been omitted by you: for Pythagoras, Archytas, Plato, and the rest of the ancient philosophers declared that the motion of the universe and the revolution of the stars do not come to be or subsist without music, saying that all things have been constructed by God according to harmony. It would be unseasonable now to prolong our discourse on this subject; for the highest and most musical thing of all is to set due measure upon everything. With these words he sang a paean, and after pouring a libation to Cronus and his children, together with all the gods and the Muses, he dismissed the guests.
